newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Dostum said to offer ceasefire to Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Dostum said to offer ceasefire to Taleban.

text.p: Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar conveyed a ceasefire offer from Uzbek leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum to Afghanistan's Taleban militia on Sunday, Taleban sources said.

The sources said Babar passed on the proposal at a 30-minute meeting with senior Taleban leaders, including Acting Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous, at the Islamic movement's headquarters in the southern city of Kandahar.
Babar, who earlier flew from Islamabad to Dostum's base in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, told them the Uzbek chief had proposed a ceasefire to take effect at noon on Monday.
"We are thinking about it," one Taleban official, Mullah Abdul Jalil, told a correspondent of the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press Agency in Kandahar.

It was not immediately clear if Dostum had offered a ceasefire only on his own behalf, or whether he was also speaking for his partners in a defence pact signed last week -- ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood and Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction leader Karim Khalili.
Pakistan, which denies charges that it supports the Taleban, has been trying to avert fighting between the Sunni Moslem militants now ruling Kabul and forces loyal to Dostum.

A spokesman for Masood said on Sunday that Dostum's troops were poised to push down the so-called new road from Bagram airbase, 60 km (40 miles) north of Kabul, but witnesses said the frontline there did not appear to have changed significantly.
Dostum's reported offer coincided with intense military pressure on the Taleban from Masood's forces, who advanced to within 20 km (13 miles) of Kabul on Sunday.
The Taleban captured the Afghan capital on September 27, but Masood withdrew his forces in fairly good order and has since struck back with some support from Dostum, his former foe.
